title: The American Dream Is Not Dead
author: Diego Torres
content:
_This editorial by Diego Torres appears as the introduction to the November
2026 issue of_ Let's Talk About Migration _(_ Hablemos de Migración _), a
magazine on migration issues published by the Frente Amplio de Mexicanos y
Migrantes.[Read and download the full November
issue](https://diegotorres72.com/internacional/boletin-hablemos-de-
migracion-2/)._

![Let's Talk About Migration](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2025/06/image-1.png)

Talking about migration also means addressing the topic of the "American
Dream." Some say the American Dream is dead, that it disappeared many years
ago, or that it has become the American nightmare. However, these assertions
stem from forgetting the underlying causes that continue to force many people
to emigrate in search of a better life.

Many of the first European settlers who arrived in what is now the United
States were seeking better living conditions or fleeing religious persecution.
The Library of Congress itself documents that several of the British colonies
in North America were established by people escaping religious persecution in
Europe, while others came seeking economic opportunities. This is not unlike
what currently motivates people to continue coming to the United States,
however dangerous the journey may be.

Migration has been a part of U.S. history since the early settlers, beginning
with Asians (primarily Chinese), Europeans, and Mexicans, all present during
the expansion of the American empire. Later came the influx of Cubans and a
significant increase in Mexicans, and continuing to this day with Africans,
Venezuelans, Haitians, Cubans, Chinese, and a long list of other
nationalities. While their circumstances differ, the reasons for their
migration are similar. Over time, many of these migrants forget what they fled
and settle for the precarious life offered by the United States, especially
for undocumented immigrants; precarious, but better than what they had in
their home communities.

And worse still, forgetting these causes means not only assimilating
xenophobic rhetoric, but also putting it into practice. Today, we see not only
migrants in uniform as ICE agents, but also pro-Trump activists who violently
attack their own people—those they themselves once were and now refuse to
acknowledge.

![The American Dream Is Not Dead](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/ltam-nov26-01-body-p05.jpg)Illustration: _Let 's Talk
About Migration_, November 2026

This passivity on the part of the majority of migrants, both documented and
undocumented, who are being harassed, persecuted, detained, and deported,
coupled with the support of a few forgetful migrants, has been exploited by
the Trump administration to fuel its hate campaign against those whom he and
many others consider inferior. This is not merely a perception. In March 2016,
the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination
expressed its concern about the language used by Donald Trump to refer to
migrants. The body warned that portraying them as criminals or as a burden on
society can incite racial discrimination and hate crimes.

Migrants are becoming victims of their own making. Their failure to organize
and demand their rights has made them easy targets for the orange-clad
dictator's attempts. Meanwhile, the consequences of this immigration policy
are visible on the streets. Reuters documented in October 2026 that, since
January 2025, at least 21 people had been shot by ICE agents and 7 had died.
One of the most recent cases occurred in New York, where a man was wounded
during an operation while his five- year-old son was inside the vehicle.

The American Dream isn't dead, it's just transformed. Governments that send
migrants away repeat it in speeches full of rhetoric but lacking substance. In
Mexico, the discourse tells migrants, "Mexico embraces you," but it fails to
acknowledge the reality that continues to drive them away. And "Mexico
Embraces You" isn't just a phrase: it's the name of the National Repatriation
Strategy, created by the Mexican government to receive Mexican nationals
returning from the United States. The Ministry of the Interior itself states
that the program offers lodging, food, medical care, and other services to
repatriated individuals. In March 2026, the government reported 189,830
returns of Mexican nationals since January 20, 2025. But it fails to mention
that a dignified and permanent return can't even be considered a dream; at
best, it's an illusion that vanishes just days after the migrant returns to
the same community that initially expelled them.

But therein lies the contradiction: Mexicans are welcomed and embraced upon
their return, but the reality that initially drove them out is rarely
acknowledged. Similarly, we can find similar narratives in many parts of the
world.

Scholars and advocates for migrants claim that the American Dream is
disappearing, but the truth is quite the opposite. It hasn't disappeared at
all; people not only continue to leave, but they also don't return of their
own free will. Because they know that if life in the United States is bad for
them, in Mexico or in the countries they come from, there is neither a present
nor a future. And as soon as the conditions arise that allow them to try to
cross the border again, they won't hesitate, and they will attempt the leap
once more.
